grow.title: Grow your money
grow.subtitle: What a savings account, a fixed deposit and a mutual fund actually are, what each one asks you to give up, and where they sit on the risk ladder.
grow.notice.title: General information, not advice
grow.notice.body: This is a beginner's guide to three ordinary ways of holding money. It explains what each one is, what it gives you and what it costs you, and then it stops. It names no product at all, on purpose: a page that tells you which bank, fund or investment to use does not belong in a budgeting app.
grow.notice.line1: Nothing on this page is a recommendation, a suggestion or a forecast.
grow.notice.line2: No return is guaranteed anywhere, on anything, ever. Interest rates change, markets fall, and how something performed in the past says nothing about how it will perform next year.
grow.notice.line3: Everything here is general information for everyone. What to do with your own money is your own decision, and a qualified adviser is the person to ask about your own situation.
grow.legend.title: The risk ladder
grow.legend.intro: All three of these sit on the same three-rung ladder. A rung describes how much the value of the money can move — not how much it might pay, and not who is offering it.
grow.legend.colourNote: The colour only repeats the word that is already there, so this page reads the same in greyscale, in high contrast and to a screen reader.
grow.risk.lowMeaning: The value holds steady and the money is normally reachable quickly. You can still lose a little to fees, or to a rate a bank decides to change.
grow.risk.mediumMeaning: The value moves up and down over months or years, and a bad run can last a long while. It only makes sense for money you can leave alone for that long.
grow.risk.highMeaning: The value can fall a long way in a short time and all of it is at risk. A large loss is a normal possibility here, not an unlucky exception.

grow.concepts.title: The three, side by side
grow.concepts.intro: In the order most students meet them. Read them together: what separates them is mostly when you can get the money back and who is holding it, not how much they pay.
grow.concept.savings.title: Savings account
grow.concept.savings.what: An account at a bank or credit union. Your money stays there, the bank pays you a little interest on it, and you can take it out whenever you want.
grow.concept.savings.point1: The interest is small, and the bank can change its rate at any time. Today's rate is not a promise about next year.
grow.concept.savings.point2: There is normally no lock-in and no penalty for changing your mind. You can usually close the account yourself, online, in a few minutes.
grow.concept.savings.point3: Some accounts pay interest only above a minimum balance, or only on the first slice of your balance and not on the rest. Read which one you are signing up for.
grow.concept.savings.point4: Money held with a regulated bank is usually covered by a deposit-protection scheme up to a legal limit. Look yours up where you live — it is a number, and it is not a large one.
grow.concept.savings.lockIn: None. You can take the money out the same day you decide you want it, which is the whole reason for keeping it here.
grow.concept.fd.title: Fixed deposit
grow.concept.fd.what: You lend money to a bank for a fixed period — three months, six months, a year — and the bank pays you a rate that is set for that whole period.
grow.concept.fd.point1: The rate cannot move during the term, so you know exactly what you get if the term runs as planned. If rates rise in the meantime you stay on the old one: that is the price of knowing.
grow.concept.fd.point2: You normally cannot take the money out before the end. Ending the term early usually costs you some or all of the interest.
grow.concept.fd.point3: At the end, the money and the interest come back — or it rolls straight into another term if you do nothing. Check which of those happens by default.
grow.concept.fd.point4: The bank is still the one holding the money, so the bank's own condition matters, not just the rate printed on the slip.
grow.concept.fd.lockIn: The whole term, usually three to twelve months. Put in only what you can genuinely leave untouched until the end.
grow.concept.fund.title: Mutual fund
grow.concept.fund.what: A pool of money from many people. A manager invests it across company shares, government bonds, or a mix of the two, and you own a piece of the pool.
grow.concept.fund.point1: The value goes up and down, and it can fall below what you put in. No return is promised, and a good year in the past is no reason to expect another.
grow.concept.fund.point2: Money you will need within the next few years is a poor fit. A bad stretch can arrive in the same month as the bill you had counted on.
grow.concept.fund.point3: Charges come off what you keep — an entry fee, an exit fee, or an annual management charge, sometimes all three. A small percentage a year works steadily against you, exactly as steadily as interest works for you.
grow.concept.fund.point4: This money is invested, not deposited, so it is not covered by deposit protection, and it usually takes a few working days to come back to you rather than a day.
grow.concept.fund.lockIn: No fixed term, but allow a few working days for the money to reach you, and check whether an exit charge applies.
grow.concept.fund.readMore: No fund, manager or share is named here on purpose. If you ever compare several, the risk level, the charges and how long you can leave the money alone are the things worth comparing.
grow.start.title: How to start
grow.start.intro: Four habits, in the order they help. None of them asks you to decide anything about a product.
grow.start.step1: Know your surplus. The figure above is income minus spending for this month, and it is the only number that tells you what you could actually put away. A plan built on a bigger number is a plan that fails in the third week.
grow.start.step2: Start small. An amount moved automatically the day you get paid is worth more than a larger amount you mean to save later. Small and boring beats large and abandoned.
grow.start.step3: Keep an emergency buffer before you put any money at risk. Savings you can reach the same day are what stop one broken phone, one course fee or one month without work from turning into debt.
grow.start.step4: Read the fine print. Lock-in, exit charges, notice periods, tax, whether deposits are protected, and what the word “guaranteed” actually covers — all of it is in the terms, not in the advert.
grow.not.title: What this page is not
grow.not.line1: It is not advice. It names no bank, fund, manager or share, and it tells you to buy, open, move or sell nothing.
grow.not.line2: It promises nothing. No number on this page is a forecast, and no return is guaranteed — not even where the word “guaranteed” is printed on something else.
grow.not.line3: It does not know your circumstances. The only thing it reads is your own ledger, to work out what is left over this month. What you do about that is your decision.
grow.more.title: Before you save, look at what comes in
grow.more.body: The other half of putting money aside is what arrives in the first place. The side-income library lists generic ways students bring in extra: tutoring, campus work, selling things you no longer use, and skills you already have.
